# Results — Study 48 (Groundhog): return seasonality on the S&P 500, 2000–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Monthly returns of **398 current S&P 500
members** with ≥20y history (Yahoo) — a **survivor panel** (see the data stamp). Each month, score
every stock by its mean return in the *upcoming calendar month* over the trailing **up to** 20 years
(≥5 same-month observations accepted, so the earliest years rank on 5–12 obs); long the top quintile,
short the bottom. As-of 2026-06; inputs fingerprint `c768f59e31fe`. (The panel cache is unchanged from
the original run — the fingerprint stands; the cost numbers below were re-derived after fixing the
turnover accounting from round-trip to one-way, and the decay labels corrected.)*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `REAL` · Tradability `FRAGILE` · "Genuinely same-month seasonal"? `CONFIRMED`

This is the rare one that **survives** — with one caveat that belongs on the *Signal* axis, not just
the tradability footnote. The claim sounds like numerology — a stock repeats its calendar-month
performance — and on this panel the long-short earns **+7.3%/yr at a Sharpe of 0.81 (Lo t = 4.1)**,
wins 64% of months, and **does not decay** (Sharpe 0.81 in both halves). But the panel is **current
S&P 500 members filtered on ≥20y of history** — survivors twice over — so that magnitude is an **upper
bound**, not an estimate. What keeps the stamp `REAL` is what survives the bias: the *same-month vs
other-month contrast* (both arms share the survivorship, and the control still earns **−3.3%/yr**),
and Heston-Sadka's original result on CRSP, which includes delisted names. Existence: well-supported.
Magnitude: inflated by construction. Tradability is `FRAGILE` and thinner than first published here:
counting turnover **one-way** (~3.2× NAV/mo for an 80%-replaced two-sided book), break-even is
**≈19 bp** and net Sharpe **0.38 at 10 bp** — before the short book's borrow fee (25–50 bp/yr trims
it to 0.33–0.36).

## Data stamp

- **Universe**: 398 current S&P 500 members, ≥20y history, hedge sample 2000-01 → 2026-06, 318
  months, fingerprint `c768f59e31fe`.
- **Survivorship, named**: the panel conditions on the future twice — *current* index membership
  (delisted losers absent) and a ≥20y-history filter. `groundhog/data.py` raises a
  `SurvivorshipBiasError` unless the caller passes `allow_survivorship_bias=True`; every number on
  this page is measured on that opted-in panel and is an upper bound on the investable magnitude.

## The effect is real — and specific to the same month

| | mean/yr | Sharpe | Lo t | hit rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **same-month seasonality** | **+7.3%** | **0.81** | **4.1** | 64% |
| control (other-month history) | −3.3% | −0.21 | −1.1 | 51% |

The same-month predictor pays strongly and significantly; ranking on *other* months' history does the
opposite. That contrast is the decisive evidence — **both arms run on the same survivor panel**, so
the bias differences out of the comparison: whatever survivorship adds, it adds to both, and only the
same month predicts. That, plus Heston & Sadka (2008) finding the effect on CRSP (delisted names
included), is why the *existence* gets `REAL` even though the +7.3%/yr headline shouldn't be taken at
face value.

### Why 0.81 here vs the published 0.340

The vendor entry ([paperswithbacktest](https://github.com/paperswithbacktest/awesome-systematic-trading))
lists the *12-Month Cycle* at Sharpe **0.340**; we print **0.81**. The gap is not a discovery — it's
the universe and the bias. We use 398 current large-cap survivors with 20+ years of history (upward
bias on any cross-sectional spread, and a quality filter to boot); published implementations use
broader, point-in-time universes over different periods, often with weighting and sector constraints.
Take 0.34 as the order of magnitude an honest implementation earned, and 0.81 as what a survivor
panel *shows* — the truth is likely nearer the former.

## It hasn't decayed

| | same-month Sharpe |
|---|---|
| 2000–2012 | **0.81** |
| 2013–on | **0.81** |

Identical across halves — unusual for a published anomaly. (The hedge sample starts 2000-01: the panel
opens 1995-01 and the scorer needs its 60-month warmup.) Note the early years rank stocks on as few as
5 same-month observations; only from the mid-2010s does the full 20-year lookback apply.

## Why tradability is `FRAGILE` — counted one-way

The book replaces ~80% of a two-sided portfolio every month. Each replacement is two one-way trades
(sell the old, buy the new) on each side: ~**3.2× NAV of one-way volume per month**. An earlier
version of this page charged 1.6× — treating the sweep as round-trip — and overstated the break-even
2× (38 bp). Corrected:

| cost (one-way) | net Sharpe |
|---|---|
| gross | 0.81 |
| 5 bp | 0.59 |
| 10 bp | **0.38** |
| 20 bp | −0.04 |
| **break-even** | **≈ 19 bp one-way** |

And the short leg (~80 names, ~1× NAV) pays borrow. At a large-cap general-collateral 25–50 bp/yr,
the 10 bp-cost net Sharpe slips from **0.38 to 0.36–0.33**. So: alive at institutional large-cap costs
(a few bp one-way), dead by ~20 bp, borrow shaves the rest — on a panel that flatters the gross to
begin with. `FRAGILE` is the honest stamp: it survives on paper, with no margin for error.

## The honest takeaway

Return seasonality is the bench's outlier: a genuinely *strange* claim whose **existence holds up** —
significant (t 4.1), same-month-specific (a control that shares the panel's bias still fails), and
undecayed — while its **magnitude, measured here, is inflated** by a twice-survivor universe. `REAL`
on existence with the caveat attached; `CONFIRMED` seasonal. After one-way turnover (~19 bp
break-even), short borrow and the survivor flatter, what you could actually bank is thin — hence
`FRAGILE`, not a free lunch. Sometimes the weird thing is true; it still isn't easy money.
